utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, and a special welcome to the Registrar. Could you call the case, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Sarah Clanton; Case Manager, Thomas Laugel; and legal interns, Moritz von Normann and Sarah Munsch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with legal intern, Milan Jovancevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: One thing from yesterday you'd inquired what was the date of your suspect interview when you had spoken about Badza, Radovan Stojicic, and we went back and looked and that was on the 2nd of March, 2002.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yesterday when we finished off, I was asking you some questions about relations between Arkan and the TO of SBWS, particularly Ilija Kojic; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we're going to shift gears a little bit now. And I'd ask if we could please see -- unfortunately, this is a document that's confidential so we need to go briefly back into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please. Private session, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, Mr. Hadzic. If you could please continue.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already told you, it was established for entire Croatia, for all the Serbs in the former Socialist Republic of Croatia. Koncarevic and Petrovic proposed the establishment of a regional national council for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and that body should have been part of the bigger, Babic's body. However, later on, the two were completely independent of each other. The latter did not become a part of Babic's council. Babic was actually against its establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so when we talk now -- what I'm going to call the SNC, the Serbian National Council, just so you know I'm only going to be asking you about the SNC for the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, okay?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You along with the two gentlemen whom you've just mentioned, Koncarevic and Petrovic, you were a founding member of the SNC; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the three of us, there were several of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I think in your direct examination you said that initially all of the members were not identified to protect their security.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. In Croatia, we probably would have been arrested, and as things stood, we still moved freely around Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the SNC for your region, SBWS, was established on the 7th of January, 1991, a secret meeting was held in a place, a small place called Sidski Banovci, I believe. You attended. And that's when the Serbian National Council was established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was commonly known.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 1939.04.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tab number is 743, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this document is entitled -- well, it is a communication or a proposal of the Serbian National Council Regional Board for SBWS. It's directed to the president of the SFRY Presidency, Mr. Jovic. And at the end, at the bottom, it's dated 3rd of February, 1991. So this would be about one month after the establishment of the SNC. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Hadzic? Do you have --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you involved in writing this or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we see the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And while we're at it, Mr. Stringer, I'm afraid that 743 is not the right tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We think it is, Mr. President. We've double-checked. 743, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at this document now, Mr. Hadzic? We can blow it up some more if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that this is a letter of Ilija Petrovic to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as of 3rd of February, 1991, what was his position in the SNC?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was appointed the spokesman from the time that the SNC was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, Mr. Hadzic, Mr. Petrovic came from Serbia, from Novi Sad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a post office employee in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Had he ever actually lived as a Serb in Croatia? Had he lived in Croatia previously?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When did you first meet Mr. Petrovic? How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think it was at the founding assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party in Novi Sad, at the Arena cinema in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And approximately when would that have occurred?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was in the summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So looking now at this document, Mr. Hadzic, 1939.04, you said -- I asked you if you recognised it. You said no. Do you recall whether you had any involvement in the discussions that are referred to in this document, things said when you first met with Petrovic and Koncarevic on the 7th of January? And we can go through the document. Maybe that's best. In paragraph 1 at the top, it says, he says that all contested -- let me start with the beginning. This is directed I think I said to Mr. Jovic with the aim of putting an end to conflicts that have lasted centuries between Croatian and Serbian people. And what's proposed, first of all, in number 1 is that contested and uncontested regions in the territory of the present Republic of Croatia be defined. And then in 1.1 he says that uncontested regions are those where Croatian statehood was established back in the middle ages and where the Serbian population has never constituted a majority. So I take it, Mr. Hadzic, do you know -- that would be a reference to the parts of Croatia that Croatian Serbs would not lay any claim to. They would not contest those areas. For example, Zagreb. Zagreb would be an uncontested region, according to this; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really comment on it. I never discussed the document, and I didn't see it at the time. I didn't even know that it was issued or that Petrovic wrote to Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He goes on in 1.2 to talk then about what the contested regions. And those are areas inhabited by the Serb population, since ancient times. And it goes on -- I'm not going -- we don't need to read it all. It's based upon a number of historical developments. And he says according to this view, in addition to Kninska Krajina and the Serbian municipalities Lika, Banja, Kordon, as well as other possible territories relevant to the delineation of borders, the contested territories include Baranja, Western Srem, from the Ilok-Lovas-Jameni line to the Cepin-Trnjani line, and Slavonia from Cepin-Trnjani line to the Ilova river and a point 10 kilometres west of Rogatica. Are these things that were discussed when you met with Mr. Petrovic and Koncarevic on 7th of January and formed this body?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that and that topic was never something at the meetings which were infrequent, and after the 7th of January, we never met. This was -- we never convened. So this was not ever discussed, as far as I know, and this is the first time I hear this nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, subsequently, you actually became the president or the chairman of the SNC. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in June, when I was elected by the full composition of the National Assembly to form the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The document continues in paragraph 2 proposing suspension of the authority of the Croatian Sabor in the contested regions. And then it goes on to say, "This jurisdiction would be in effect ...," talking about placing these contested regions under the direct jurisdiction of the SFRY Presidency and federal SUP. It say: "This jurisdiction would be in effect until precise criteria for the delineation of borders between the Serbian and Croatian peoples are determined, including the voluntary relocation of all interested Serbs, Croats, and members of the different national minorities inhabiting these regions across the line which would be established as the future border between the Croatian national state and Yugoslavia. Any other interested citizens currently residing east or west of the border of the contested territories as outlined here may avail themselves of the right to voluntary relocation." Now, Mr. Petrovic being the spokesperson of the SNC, Mr. Hadzic, I'm going to suggest to you that what is happening here is that he is articulating precisely what is the platform for the objective of the SNC which is to establish a line of separation between Croatian and Serbian people and then to facilitate population movement to create homogenous ethnic populations on either side of the line. Was that the objective of the SNC?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the goal. What you believe is one thing, but that is not correct. And this is what Ilija Petrovic was talking about. I had no idea about it, and I cannot even comment. If I were a lawyer, perhaps I could speak about the legal aspects of it; but I'm not, so I cannot. I know as much as you do about it, nothing special. The Serbian National Council was formed in order to represent the interests of the Serbian people because it was said that the Serbian Democratic Party could not do that because not all Serbs were members of the SDS. So I was not -- I reluctantly agreed to attend meetings of the SNC but this was not something that was ever discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What you're saying here is that Mr. Petrovic's articulating his own personal opinion or view as to what the SNC should be advocating?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume so, because I don't know anything about it. And this was not something that was discussed at any of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tendered this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object due to lack of foundation because the witness testified that he doesn't know anything being the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would say that Mr. Hadzic has in fact agreed, identified Mr. Petrovic as the spokesperson of the SNC and has indicated that apparently the views expressed in this are those of Mr. Petrovic who was associated with Mr. Hadzic in the SNC. And so we think that is a sufficient basis for admitting the document in terms of its showing or giving some indication of what the SNC is about at the time of its establishment in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, this document is an extract from a book; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This comes from the Petrovic book. Other documents from it are already in evidence through the witness, Mr. Nielson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 388, which is L0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And while it's coming up, Mr. Hadzic, this is the declaration on sovereign autonomy of the Serb people of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. You were asked about this document in your direct examination. And at transcript page 9436, you said that you didn't have anything to do with this. Can we agree, Mr. Hadzic, that as is indicated here in the original language version, the document's actually published in the Official Gazette of the SBWS that came out at the end of 1991. Do you agree with me, it was actually published in the Gazette?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to Article 7. Mr. Hadzic, the document is talking about autonomy issues. This is in Article 6. Serbs asserting autonomy in respect of certain issues, Serbs in Croatia. And then this in Article 7, it says that until the conditions for foundation and norm functioning of autonomy bodies are established, their duties will be carried out by the Serb National Council ... the national council has the right to declare null and void all legal documents which insult current constitution of Yugoslavia and sovereign autonomy of the Serb people in SBWS. The question here, Mr. Hadzic, is -- and I know you say you didn't have any -- you don't associate yourself with this document. Does this give us an indication of what was envisaged for the SNC that it would function as a sort of governmental body until such time as Serbs in Croatia were able to organise themselves into more formal governmental structures such as the assembly, the government, the ministries and other things that came later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know about that so I am really not able to interpret any of this. I didn't ever even think about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you said that the Serb National Council, I believe you said that it was created in order to exist outside of parties, that it was intended to unite terms, I guess, of party affiliations. Can we agree on that as a basic element of the SNC?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that to be an institution that was supposed to represent the interests of the people in the Serbian territory. But I didn't really go into any legal predictions or I wasn't really very versed in these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- I think that the translation is wrong. He said of the people -- of the Serbian people in the territory not the people in the Serbian territory. Serbian people in the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Hadzic confirm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I said. Yes, there was no Serbian territory. Croats and Serbs were mixed in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Since you say you didn't have anything to do with this, Mr. Hadzic, would this have also come from Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out when I came here that this was written by a doctor of legal sciences who was born in Nis. But I don't know who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, somehow, Mr. Hadzic, it found its way into the Official Gazette of the SBWS, which a few months after this, you're its prime minister. Doesn't this in fact articulate again what was the vision or the objective of the SNC at this stage as a body that would take on governmental functions until the conditions for foundation and normal functioning of autonomous bodies are established?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I am accused of very serious matters here, of which I'm not guilty, I would like to tell you most sincerely when the Serbian National Council was established, I couldn't assume that a war would break out or what would happen would happen. What happened is, they said there was a need for somebody to represent Serbian interests. I saw in Croatia that nobody would come forward and represent the interests of the Serbs so I did that myself. But I didn't even dream of the possibility that it would come to war. Our party's position to which I belonged and Professor Raskovic belonged is that as many --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Hadzic please repeat the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was our position, the position of the party that I belonged to, and this is something that Professor Raskovic repeated, to the extent that Croatia is in Yugoslavia to the same extent Serbs would be in Croatia. This was something well-known. I only knew that and this was my starting political position. And for those reasons right up until the war I kept in contact with Croatia in order to prevent its secession and also to prevent possible conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You have been saying that SNC was established to represent the interests of the Serbs. Can you give me one concrete thing that it did or that it wanted to do in order to represent Serbian interests?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one thing. I said in my previous answer to prevent any possible conflicts, not to prevent war. Because I didn't even -- it didn't even occur to me that it would come to war. But in the transcript it says war. I mean, I think I know English that well. I would now just like to ask you to repeat your question because I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question was: You have been saying that the SNC was established to represent the interests of the Serbs. Can you give me one concrete example of what it did or what it wanted to do in order to represent Serbian interests.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since you're asking for an example, I think that there is actually just one, and that is that in the territory of Vojvodina we organised the receipt of refugees from Slavonia and Baranja in an organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Didn't the SNC have territorial aspirations? That is, it wished to identify parts of Croatia that would be autonomous Serbian areas and to delineate those areas in a territorial way?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was never discussed at meetings. I saw that when I came here, in Ilija Petrovic's book, and that was the first time that I heard of the geographic term "Moslavina." To tell you the truth, I don't even know today exactly where this territory is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you say again the geographic term you just said. The interpreter -- or the court reporter would like to get it. Now I'm seeing Moslavina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moslavina. Yes, you are right. Moslavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we move to Article 9 of this document. Again, for the record, it is L0001, declaration on sovereign autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking about territorial aspirations because here we see that in this declaration, it is purporting to extend autonomy through local government to those municipalities and local communities where Serbs have majority now or where they had majority in -- on April 6, 1941. Now the reference to the 6th of April, 1941, this, Mr. Hadzic, is a reference to Croats who came from elsewhere during the Pavelic years in 1941. There is a talk about Croats who arrived from Herzegovina, down in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were settled during the Second World War period when Pavelic and the NDH existed. Is that what this is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't know anything about this document but I do know about the 6th of April, unrelated to this document. So I'm just going to say for the benefit of the Trial Chamber what happened on the 6th of April. On the 6th of April, Fascist Germany attacked the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and World War II began in the whole of the former Yugoslavia and also in the area where I was born. From the 6th of April until the liberation from Fascism, the Serbian people experienced genocide. They had almost a million victims in that war, along with the Jews, with the Roma. It was those three peoples who were the victims during the war in that area. Since I know what I am saying from other sources and on the basis of other information and even though I'm not a lawyer, I did hear that the consequences of genocide must be taken into account and no rights can be acquired through consequences of genocide. So the date of April 6th when the Germans attacked has nothing to do with the formation of the independent state of Croatia which was later. But it has even less to do with resettlement of population. This happened after April the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So according to this declaration on sovereign autonomy, then, I'm going to put it you, Mr. Hadzic, the SNC, its goal was to restore Serbian -- well, let me say it this way: To restore the demographic composition of those areas falling within its territory to that which existed prior to World War II, prior to the genocide against the Serbs and prior to the arrival of Croats from elsewhere; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. That would have been impossible. I was simply trying to provide an interpretation with regard to the date of 6th of April. I don't know what the true goal of this declaration was because, as I said already, I had no clue about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 1939.13, tab 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Hadzic, just one last question about this previously document, the declaration on sovereign autonomy. Transcript page 9436 in this trial, you said on your direct examination: "I remember that declaration but I was made aware of it later. In February, I didn't really attach any importance to it. I didn't even know what it represented. I did not take part in it." The question is: When did you become aware of this sovereign declaration on autonomy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became aware of it later on. I'm not sure whether it was before I arrived here or only upon my arrival. I do remember, however, that when I provided my statement to the investigators in 2002, Koncarevic Ilija came to see me, to ask me what happened. I didn't even realise he was aware of me talking to the investigators. We talked about it and he said, Well, you're not guilty. You don't even have to answer questions, you just have to say that you followed the declaration. I said, What declaration? He said, The declaration on autonomy. And I think that was the first I heard of it. I had nothing to do with it. I was unaware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In June of 1991, you were elected as the prime minister designate for SBWS, and in September, on 25th of 1991, you actually became the prime minister. At no time did you become aware of this document or the fact that it was published in your own Gazette in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. My obligations had to do with the Vance Plan at that time, and I don't remember anyone informing me about it. I didn't pay much attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could now look at the document on the screen, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is also from the Petrovic book. 65 ter 1939.13.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you elected as the chairman of the SNC on the 17th of March, 1991, which is what's indicated here, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. And I did not even attend any SNC meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you say you're not present at this meeting, or the session that occurred on the 17th of March in Sid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not even sure it took place. But even if it did, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No one told you that you were now -- someone had decided that you would be chairman of the SNC?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me. They tried to talk me into accepting it as early as the 7th of January, and I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 1D02959, which is tab 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm going to put it to you that you're not being truthful about this, that in fact you did become chairman of the SNC at that time. This is an article from the 10th of April, 1991. And in the English, starting about halfway down the first paragraph: "The conditions brought forward by the so-called Serbian National Council are well known to the public from before, and as almost all of them in the form of an ultimatum, it is hard to believe the possible talks would last shortly." Just -- this is from "Vecernje List," Mr. Hadzic. This is a Croatian publication; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the article continues: "Goran Hadzic, one of the leading SDS persons for SBWS, as well as the president of the so-called Serbian National Council, also announced that negotiations would last long."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we zoom in the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me know when you're ready to take a question, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, what is the basis of your conclusion that I was lying? Based on what was published in a Croatian paper? I was arrested after this. What was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is the 10th of April. It is after Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that, I went to see Bojlkovac [phoen] and Degoricija in Zagreb. Had I been SNC president, I would have been arrested and left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It was publicly known that you were the president of the SNC as of 10th of April, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that kind of information. And I am not aware of that SNC decision if it met at all. This is the first I hear of it, from you. I guess someone must have made that decision without me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, is it just a coincidence then that the people who are writing this article, they seem to know that you're president of the SNC as of April. This is news to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had that been true, I would have been arrested by Croatian authorities. The SNC was a para state organisation which was not allowed under the Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. President [sic], you were arrested by Croatian authorities, weren't you, on the 31st of March, in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying that I was arrested because I was a member of the SNC? I think I explained that and that everyone knows about it. I was arrested by mistake and I was not arrested for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that. We just looked at 1939.13 which is from the Petrovic book, a document indicating that you been elected chairman of the SNC, and I understand that you don't accept that. But about two weeks after that, then, you find yourself in Obrovac at a SDS meeting, on the 31st of March; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation I received was that happened two weeks later. But in my understanding, it was two weeks before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm saying two weeks from the 17th of March, approximately.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you had the 10th of April in mind. I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You and Mr. Savic travelled down there. And in your direct testimony at page 9385, you said that what happened at Plitvice was completely by chance?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have P00071.50, which is tab 151.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is a report from the media dated 29th of March, 1991, at Plitvice. It refers to the co-ordination commission of the Executive Council of Titova Korenica municipality implementing the decision on transforming Plitvice Lakes National Park into the Krajina public enterprise. It continues both administrative buildings of the national park were taken over with the help of Knin policemen. The commission handed in dismissal noticed to the following five members of the board. Although the hotels in the park are open, guests are not coming. It has been learned that 80 per cent of reservations have been cancelled. Mr. Hadzic, what's being referred to here is that Milan Martic and police of the Knin Krajina Autonomous District had, on the 29th of March, actually taken over the Plitvice National Park area; correct? That did happen on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, but that's what one can read in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in fact it's a well-known national park, popular with tourists. But a lot of the tourists knew about what had happened there because they were cancelling their reservations, and they weren't going to Plitvice. Did you in fact know in advance when you went to the SDS meeting in Obrovac that Martic had taken over the Plitvice National Parks area and it was not just a coincidence that you went there on the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is compound question. He could not -- if he could be -- could be divided in two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you break it down, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you in advance -- when you went to the SDS meeting in Obrovac -- did you learn when you were in Obrovac that Martic and his people had taken over Plitvice National Park?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I am testifying under oath, I cannot tell you precisely. It is possible that I heard about it at the meeting, although I am not sure. I did not pay much attention to it. It had nothing to do with me or with Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, this in fact was a tremendous event wasn't it? Martic and the police of the SAO Krajina actually taking over control -- setting up barricades at Plitvice. I put it to you, sir, that you would not have known about it when you were attending the SDS meeting in Obrovac which was itself in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All you said was a presumption. At the meeting in Obrovac there were only SDS members. Martic was not a SDS member. I arrived at the meeting as asked to do by the Croatian police to be -- to take up a position which ran counter to Martic's position in political and all other terms. I explained that, and I enumerated the people I talked to before my travel to Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so it was just a coincidence, then, that you found yourself at Plitvice two days after it was taken over by Martic and the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't believe that you think it was not a coincidence. Even Borivoje Savic testified to that effect, although he said many other things that were gibberish. But he also confirmed that it was a coincidence. In addition to us being there, there were another 2 to 300 tourists. There were two busloads of Italian tourists, double-deckers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have tab 152, which is P00020.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I see a stamp in the left corner, left upper corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It was initially provided under Rule 54 bis. It was subsequently released for public use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this comes from the Serbian government. It was an analysis that was prepared of the operations, the events that took place at Plitvice on the 31st of March, 1991. Under paragraph number 1, "Causes of the conflict," it talks first about events, developments that occurred on the Croatian side, which we've heard about a lot in the -- in the trial, Croatia's new constitution, arms imports, cessation from Yugoslavia, all of that. And then in the next paragraph, it says: "The immediate reason for the armed clash in Plitvice was the decision of the Titova Korenica municipality to declare the... lakes a publicly owned enterprise of the so-called SAO Krajina, demonstrating its readiness to defend the area even if that meant... armed conflict." Mr. Hadzic, is it your testimony that when you were attending the SDS meeting in Obrovac, you were not aware of these events, the declaration on making Plitvice part of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I've said already. I am not certain I had heard about it. I'm testifying under oath. I don't think anyone discussed it or mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please move to page 4 of the English. It's item number 6. I don't have the B/C/S page reference, but it's item number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Item number 6 is propaganda support for the armed incident: Number 1, Croatian leadership; and number 2, Serbian National Council of the SAO Krajina. Now, again, Mr. Hadzic, just so we're clear, this is a different SNC. This is not the one that we've been talking about for SBWS. Reference here, right, is to the other one for Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in the third paragraph there that begins, "On 30 March, 1991 ...," it's talking about events and the leadup to the conflict on the 31st. Croatia issues an ultimatum, makes it clear MUP forces will intervene if the SAO Krajina forces does not withdraw. And then it continues: "The SAO Krajina leadership learned that MUP forces were preparing to intervene on 29 March ... and mobilise the reserve public [sic] forces in Knin, Donji Lapac, Srb and Gracac, Titova Korenica and elsewhere, and launched a broad propaganda campaign to prepare volunteers for the defence, and on 30 March, 1991, the complete reserve police force and all civilians with a fire-arm were mobilised." It's the 30th of March. Were you not aware of this when you arrived in Obrovac and attended the SDS meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the fifth time today, I say I was not aware of it. I was not aware of those details. I see them now for the first time, and I did not get involved in it. I simply did not have information. After the meeting, a security officer of Martic's police from the SAO Krajina tried to interrogate us. That is why my colleague and I did not even want to stay in Obrovac but we wanted to go as close to Zagreb as possible to spend the night, to get away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1577, D00116. Mr. President, it's a confidential document so we'd need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, the tab number, 229, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But the -- the exhibit number I have on -- on your list for tab 229 is not the one you mentioned here on the record, but what is the nature of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It is a publication called "Pobjeda" dated 20 of September. It is 65 ter 310. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm in the wrong list. 229. Yeah. It's okay. Sorry about that, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We have a list of lists, actually, which shows how easy it is to get lost in the lists and the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is jumping ahead until the 20th of September, 1991, and you commented on this during your direct examination. I'd just like to bring you back to it for a couple of questions. The third paragraph mentions Ilija Petrovic, and this now being September 1991, I know it's not quite the 25th of September, which is the big day, but here this is indicating Mr. Petrovic is the information minister in Hadzic's government. And here the article notes that he recalled the proposal of the Serbian National Council of these districts was to establish the contentious western borders along the Ilova-Virovitica stretch if necessary by moving the Serbian and Croatian populations. Now since he is a member of your government, Mr. Hadzic, isn't he in fact articulating the policy of the government of SBWS in regard to the establishment of this territory, this western border and, if necessary, movement of Serbian and Croatian populations? Wasn't that, by now, government policy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our government never discussed that. This is Ilija Petrovic's talking about his own views on some Serb territories. Our government did not have any jurisdiction in that area, and it never discussed this. This is at the extreme western end of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You never removed him. I haven't seen anything indicating you criticised him or retreated from what he is saying publicly as your information minister. So what did you do to correct what he is saying here, if it's in fact a misstatement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was talking about his own opinions. He did have a portfolio at the time even though the government was not established yet. It was being established. It was not my government. I was not the prime minister designate. We were all equal, and appointed by the assembly. So I was not watching over what they were saying and quickly moving to correct what they were saying. Ilija Petrovic was talking about territories that were 200 kilometres away from the territory that we were responsible for, and had nothing to do with the government, nor did we ever discuss them. I don't even remember that he was saying these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is the 20th of September --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is line 25, page 46, it reads, "I was not the prime minister designate." I don't think that the witness said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can clarify that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, in terms of your position during this period of time, is it correct that in June of 1991 you became the prime minister designate? You didn't actually take up the post of prime minister until the 25th of September, however; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But it's not -- I just said that I was not the caretaker of any minister. They were all independent, they had their own portfolios, and they were all free to give any statements that they wanted. I couldn't stand behind each one of them and control them. That was not my job. So when I said this that is stated in the transcript, prime minister designate, what I meant to say was that I was not their caretaker, but I was the prime minister designate, and I was given that position which I took up on the 25th of September; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You selected Mr. Petrovic and put him forward to be the information minister of your government; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the formal sense, yes. But it was not my independent decision. It was also a result of the proposal of the rest of those who were at the meeting, the president of the assembly, Koncarevic, and some others with whom we agreed about -- but the Assembly of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was the one that made its decision on their appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please move back to a document we've looked at already, which is 65 ter 1939.04, which is tab 743. And to go to -- well, we can start at the bottom of page 1 of the document again. This is the end of paragraph 1 of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In this document - we looked at this earlier - this SNC document, that's referring to, at the bottom of page 1, the contested regions, possible territories relevant to the delineation of borders saying what the contested territories are. And here we see at the top of page 2 of the English, which is the last sentence of paragraph 1 of the B/C/S version, it's referring to this Ilok-Lovas-Jamena line, Cepin-Trnjani line, and Slavonia, Cepin-Trnjani line to the Ilova river, and a point 10 kilometres west of Rogatica. Now it's no coincidence, Mr. Hadzic, isn't it, that now your minister of information is going public with essentially the same western border proposed by the Serbian National Council, which is set out in the February document here, 1939.04. Only it's not just the Serbian National Council now, Mr. Petrovic. It's Mr. Petrovic in his capacity as minister of information who is advocating and setting out the position of your government on the establishment of this western border. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, not. It's not a coincidence. If you look carefully below this letter to President Jovic is the signature of Ilija Petrovic. And in the journalist's article, it's also Ilija Petrovic. So he is providing his opinion in this document and in the other document. In both documents, he is speaking on his on behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting to you, sir, that in fact what he is doing is he is articulating the position of your government. He is one of your ministers. You selected him and put him forward into this position. And you did that because he shared your view and was going to carry out and advocate the policy of your government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is again a compound question. And if it could be divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll do that, Mr. President. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, isn't he articulating the position of your government here, not his own personal view?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because at the time the government had not convened yet, and this was not discussed. We did not discuss this matter at our government meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if Croats out in the western part of these areas, Eastern Slavonia, are reading this and are concluding that in fact your government and the SAO SBWS has designs on taking that territory, they would have been mistaken because only they're reading the opinion of one person and not your policy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I object. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'll allow it, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, the question was essentially the effect of this on a reader who is a Croat who lives out in the western part of Eastern Slavonia who is now reading these words, you're saying that they're just reading the opinion of one person and not the policy of your government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how anybody would think about that. I didn't really pay any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you're the president of the government, Mr. Hadzic. Isn't it your job to pay attention to that? I mean, these are people. They might not be Serbs but they are people who happen to live within the borders that your government is claiming for itself. Don't you have any obligation to think about them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. But I didn't feel that they were jeopardised in any way by Mr. Petrovic's positions. That's were his personal positions and he never referred to them in government. The government didn't discuss them. That government didn't exist at the time. The government didn't exist throughout that whole 1991 period. In the sense that it would have been able to do anything. It was just in the process of being formed, and it existed on paper only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Hadzic, the government, your government, did two things quite well during this period. One was to make public statements about the objectives of your government; and the other thing it did quite well was to pass laws. And we're going to be talking about that shortly. But isn't it true that you and other members of your government made public statements and passed laws during 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did give public statements. The government adopted laws and was preparing for the eventual peace and for us to be able to remain as a region within Yugoslavia because at the time we didn't have any military or any other power to be able to implement those laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have tab 1034. This is video. P00040. And we'll wait for the interpreters to let us know when they've got it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: The issue of western borders of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is open. This was said by the president of the government of these regions, Goran Hadzic, in his talks with journalists in the Belgrade international press centre. On this occasion, he reminded about the proposal of the Serbian National Council of these areas to, if need be, establish this border with the help of moving Croatian and Serb population in the broader area. "Serb Autonomous Region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is no longer in Croatia. The issue of western borders is open and the government of this Serb autonomous region advocates a democratic way of solving this and by respecting the will of the people. Goran Hadzic, president of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, told this to local and foreign journalists in the international press centre in Belgrade. Information Minister Ilija Petrovic reminded the borders according to the London contract are Ilova-Moslavina-Virovitica, and then also at the proposal of the national council ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we've stopped it there just briefly. Can you identify the two gentlemen that we're seeing on the screen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Petrovic is on the left side with beard, and to the right, is Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: ... that the Croatian state assess whether one of the solutions would be moving of Serb and Croatian population. When asked by the journalists whether the tanks have been summoned from Belgrade, Goran Hadzic replied: 'The tanks belong to the JNA and I can tell that you within the borders of the present Republic of Croatia, JNA is if not in greater peril, than equally perilled as the Serb people living in it. They go there to liberate their colleagues, soldiers." When asked several times about who was invited to return to these region, Hadzic expressed the wish for return not only of Serbs but of native Croats as well. Serb people did not endure genocide by the native Croats but by the colonists Ante Pavelic brought to Western Herzegovina, Croatian Zagorje and Imotsko. They were the first ones to raise arms and mine Serb houses. In order to establish a normal life, we will have to present them with a return ticket. Hadzic also said Serbia should take care of women and children refugees and not of able-bodied men. Stating the data on SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Goran Hadzic stressed that there were 150.000 inhabitants living there and that its capital is Vukovar, which had not been liberated yet, but this did not mean it would not be. Goran Hadzic replied to the TAS reporter that his government offered 20 imprisoned guards to Croatian authorities in exchange for two missing Soviet journalists. 'Unfortunately,' Hadzic said, 'our government does not know where they are.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic we'll start with this and work backwards and perhaps we could -- if the transcript is not on the screen we could put it on the screen so that we can refer to it. You actually testified about this in your direct examination, I believe, with regard to the 20 imprisoned guards that you commented on here. Do you recall talking about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I heard it again just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to recap my understanding of your evidence, your testimony on that, is that prisoners, Croatian prisoners or non-Serb prisoners, in SBWS territory would not have been your responsibility but were in fact the responsibility of the JNA. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, and that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It was your government's position that Vukovar was to be the capital of the SBWS. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That Vukovar should be the capital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall offhand what was the ethnic composition of Vukovar prior to the conflict? Was it roughly 36 per cent Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last census before the war, it was 36 per cent of Serbs formally but there was a large number of Yugoslavs or those who declared themselves so but they were Serbs. So that means that the percentage of Serbs was 50 per cent, perhaps even higher when you include those Yugoslavs who wished to remain in Yugoslavia. And this is logical, because they did declare themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll probably talk about this more later. In the census in the former Yugoslavia people could decide how to declare themselves Yugoslav, Serb, Croat, Hungarian; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So for you to get to 50 per cent of Vukovar being comprised of Serbs then, you're assuming that all of the people who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs were in fact of Serbian ethnicity. But you don't really know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. I simply wanted to answer your question, but I didn't really think about that much. I didn't deal with that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, does that mean that in fact it's not correct, or you misspoke when you said that a large number of Yugoslavs or those who declared themselves so were Serbs and so that it made the percentage of Serbs in Vukovar 50 per cent. I mean, the fact is you don't really know, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be correct or precise to the 1 per cent. But it's a fact that most of those who declared themselves as Yugoslav and those who I know were Serbs or were from mixed marriages, and with one part -- one parent, the mother or the father, being a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on page 1 of the English, it's the second full paragraph of the transcript here of this video, again, the -- and I know it's the reporter speaking, but the reporter in this video footage from this press conference in Belgrade is again attributing to Mr. Petrovic statements about the establishment of borders according to the London contract along this Ilova-Moslavina-Virovitica line. So, again, what we're seeing, since he is seated next to you at the table in Belgrade at the international press centre on television, is that he is expressing not just his personal opinion but, in fact, the position of the SBWS government; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know from all of this is only that London is the capital of Great Britain. As for who signed this contract and how this came about, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Setting aside the London contract, I'm simply asking you here in -- when the report is that at this press conference in Belgrade, Petrovic is reminding of the borders being Ilova-Moslavina-Virovitica, what he is doing there is setting out the position of your government as to what the western border of SBWS should be. It's not his personal opinion; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the fifth or sixth time, I say that this was not a policy of the SBWS government. We did not discuss that. Ilija Petrovic expressed his view of the London treaty on some historical matters that I was unaware of. I didn't know about them. I don't even know what the London treaty was about and whether it was signed before World War I or World War II, or after. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you accept no responsibility for the public statements that are being made in your presence by members of your government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was before the government was established and before the appointment of ministers. The government never discussed matters concerning Western Slavonia, at least not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if you knew that this was Mr. Petrovic's personal opinion, his personal view, that from what we've seen now as being expressed repeatedly, going back to February and the letter to President Jovic, you must have shared that view by inviting him and accepting him into your government five days later. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the February letter, I didn't even know about it, the one he send to President Jovic. I wasn't notified of it. I didn't know about it and I only learned about it from his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as we see again, it's also the position of the SBWS government that the establishment of this border is going to be accompanied by population exchanges. And if it wasn't to be a policy of the SBWS government, then, in fact, you would not have accepted Mr. Petrovic into your government. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SBWS government discussed the issue of five municipalities: The former municipality of Osijek with its seat in Dalj and Tenja; the former Vinkovci municipality with its seat in Mirkovci; and the municipality of Vukovar, its entire territory; as well as the municipality of Beli Manastir. We never discussed Moslavina, Virovitica or any of the things that I can see before me now. I understood it to be some of Petrovic's gibberish since he was not a historian but always said that he was versed in history and often referred to the London treaties and such things. But it was not a topic I discussed with Petrovic or anybody else. I really had no clue about the concept of the London treaty. I didn't know when it was signed and what it was about. As for the territory of Virovitica and Moslavina, as I said, I think it is some 200 to 250 kilometres away. So if you go through the entire Western Slavonia and go to its far end closest to Zagreb, that's how far it was and it was not at all within our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What Mr. Petrovic is talking about here is a line that is quite similar to the line that's always or often associated with the position expressed by Mr. Seselj; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that as well as I do. Mr. Petrovic is still living. Thank God. So why do I need to provide answers about something he said and particularly because I wasn't aware of it. These were his personal views.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to argue with you, but you were aware of if because he is saying it publicly in a press at a televised press conference where he's seated to your right. So in fact you knew quite well what his personal views were, if in fact they were his personal views?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it as his personal views, private matter, that he mentioned at the press conference. He also sent that letter without anyone's knowledge. He sent letters throughout the former Yugoslavia and all over the world without anyone knowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go back now to the actual video itself, P00040, just a couple of last questions to finish it off, and we don't actually even need the audio. I just want to ask Mr. Hadzic about a couple of the other people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Hadzic, again, if you could indicate who we're seeing on the left and then second from the left. Who are these two gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Petrovic and Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then if we could just let it run.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you identify the gentleman who is seated to your left?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an employee of the international press centre and an interpreter from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And one last item on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 4872.2. And, Mr. President, there is no tab for this because it comes from the video. You'll -- you'll see in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hadzic, just for the record if could you tell us who are these two gentlemen and then I'm going to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From left to right, Ilija Petrovic and Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We tendered that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P3213. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's one minute early, but this would be a good time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just inform the Chamber that one of our documents were admitted -- one of our document -- documents were -- was erroneously admitted into evidence as it is 1D -- sorry. Just to see that. It is 1D1758. It was admitted as D151 and -- but 1D1768 had to be admitted as D151. And I'm grateful to the Prosecution because they warned us about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it is the document number that was wrong; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Document what is admitted into evidence is 1D1758 and it was admitted as D151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it 1D1768 has to be admitted as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Under the same document number, under the same exhibit number, we have to put 1D1768.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 1D1768 should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I would just add that the -- the accused responded in direct examination as to his relationship with Mr. Kertes on 10th of July, at page 9710.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. In fact, we were going to mention that as well. Apologies. It was my mistake. Mr. Hadzic did, indeed, testify in direct about having known Mr. Kertes before. Still our position that he did not testify about the assistance in relocating his family. But we did want to make that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 388, which is L0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is coming up. This is the Gazette that contains the laws from 1991 for the SBWS, and I want to ask you about some of those laws. Here we see at the very beginning is the declaration on sovereign autonomy of the Serb people of SBWS, and I already asked you about that. And so we're going to skip over that document and then move to the next document that appears in the Gazette at page 2 of the B/C/S, page 3 of the English. It's the decision on position of the Serb people from SBWS in the Yugoslav state community. And this is dated the 25th of June, 1991. And, Mr. Hadzic, just to refresh us, can you tell the Chamber what occurred on the 25th of June, 1991? This refers to a session of the Great National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of June, the Croatian parliament passed the decision on the separation of Croatia from Yugoslavia. At that same time, the Great National Assembly of the Serbian people passed the decision for us to separate from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is that what this decision is that we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. All I can see is the decision. I can't see anything above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It says: "Taking the right of the Serb people to self-determination as a starting point, including the right to cessation." Is this the document that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, also on the 25th of June, 1991, first of all, let me ask you: The session that is referred to here held on the 25th of June, 1992, where did that session take place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And also on the 25th of June, Mr. Hadzic, is it correct that it was on that day that you were put forth or appointed as the prime minister designate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The proposal came from the Great National Assembly and my name was put up as the prime minister designate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we see here in Article 2 that on this day, it was decided that on the territory of the SBWS, essentially the constitution and the laws of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be applied.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wanted to direct your attention to Article 5 of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It says: "As of the say of cessation or, in other words, separation of Croatia, the Serb people and some part of other nations and minorities living on the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem shall remain within a single state of the Serb people and other Yugoslav nations which opt for such state community." My first question here, Mr. Hadzic, is: As of 25th of June, 1991, on this day, what was the territory of SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it was the territory inhabited by the Serbian people in the Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can we agree that in much of the territory of the SBWS as is also the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina, actually Serb people were living with Croatian people and other Serbs, or that you had villages of Croats and Serbs that were in very close proximity to each other throughout the entire region?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the situation was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I rarely went there. However, in Slavonia and Baranja, there was a group of pure Serb villages. For example, my native village was like that. In some parts, there were villages where the population was mixed and there was also the third type, with only Croatian population. I think I made a mistake. I wanted to say that there were pure Serb villages, pure Croatian villages, and there were also mixed villages where Croats and Serbs lived together in various ratios.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's a fact that despite what is said here in Article 5, there aren't any other Yugoslav nations that were given an opportunity to opt for - that is, to choose - to be a part of this state community, this Serb district or entity that you were creating. The non-Serbs didn't get a chance to elect whether they wanted to be in that or outside of that. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. Could you please repeat it? Maybe you can shorten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, earlier you said that in Vukovar 36 per cent of the people who lived there had declared themselves to be Serbs. Did the people in Vukovar who declared themselves to be Croats ever get a chance to opt in or opt out of this SBWS territory that was being established on this day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a referendum in Croatia. Croats voted in favour of an independent Croatian state by a large majority. At the same time, Serbs had their own referendum, and a large percentage, almost 100 per cent of them, showed in that referendum that they didn't want to stay in the independent Croatian state. I have to emphasise that Croatia was the one that made the first step and seceded from Yugoslavia. Whereas, Serbs and other nations and national minorities, many of them wanted to remain in -- in Yugoslavia. It's very clear who made the first step and who wanted to go on living like before the 25th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so, in fact, you knew here on the 25th of June, and even earlier, that the strong likelihood was that Croat, perhaps other non-Serbs who lived in the SBWS, were not going to choose to be a part of the Serbian District that you were creating. You knew from the start. No one was going to opt in, if they weren't Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your question is worded in a very strange way. The Serbian people in the Socialist Republic of Croatia was a constituent people and they were equal to the Croatian people there. After the democratic elections in Croatia, the Croatian parliament unilaterally, against the will of the Serbian people, changed the constitution and passed the decision according to which the only constituent people in Croatia were Croatians and that all the others were national minorities. In keeping with the right of any people to self-determination --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I apologise for cutting you off there, but we know about that. We know about the changes to the Croatian constitution. We know about how the status of the peoples's constituent nations in Croatia changed under the constitution. I'm asking you something that is actually more practical and realistic, and the reality is that where it says that -- here other Yugoslav nations would have an opportunity to opt for or choose this, the fact is that most of the people in the region had already chosen and they had chosen to go a different direction. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that in Slavonia and Baranja a majority opted for that. A lot of people in Croatia, including Vukovar, including the municipal assembly, opted in favour of staying in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't mean that Croatian people living in Vukovar opted in favour of living in a Serbian Autonomous District of SBWS with Vukovar as its capital, did they? They certainly didn't choose that. It was imposed on them.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, nobody even mentioned that Vukovar might be the capital. We only reacted to what Croatia did. I have to say, since I'm under oath, that I'm nearly 100 per cent sure that this session of the Great National Assembly in Backa Palanka was held on the 26th of June, not on the 25th of June. I don't know why somebody thought it was on the 25th of June. That was without my knowledge. We held that meeting or the session of the Great National Assembly one day after the session of the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But you're not denying, sir that this document was adopted on that day, either the 25th or the 26th of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not denying that. Just for the sake of truth, I'm saying that it was on the 26th of June in Backa Palanka. Only later did I hear and read that it was published that it was on the 25th of June in Borovo Selo, which is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document in this -- the Gazette is something called the constitutional law of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. This is still at tab 388, L00001. And if you look at the -- the heading or the preamble, you can see, Mr. Hadzic, toward the bottom that this, according to the Gazette, is dated 25th of September, 1991. This refers to a second session of the Great National Assembly in Beli Manastir on 25th of September. Do you recall, sir, that that's the day when this constitutional law was passed by the Great National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. That's when the government was elected as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's the day that you were formally -- you formally took your office as prime minister and other ministers were also approved by the Great National Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In Article 4 here of the constitutional law, it says: "The territory of the Serb district is composed of towns, villages, places and territory where citizens made decision on integration." As of this day, 25 September, 1991, had the citizens of Vukovar made a decision on integration? And by "citizens," I mean all of the citizens of Vukovar, regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the Serbs voted in the referendum. I don't know. I was not involved in the drafting of this constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What about Ilok? Do you know if the people living in Ilok had made a decision on integration in the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is they didn't, did they? We know that they never passed any decision on integration in the SBWS. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they passed a decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, the decision that they passed is the one that came in the following month of October, when they had the referendum to leave, as the JNA and Serb forces took control of Western Srem. Isn't that the decision that was ultimately made in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that just like you. However, in your question, I can hear "the Serb forces." According to what I know, those forces were solely the JNA. There were no other Serb forces. So your term "the Serb forces" is superfluous. The only military that existed at the time was the JNA, and that was, indeed,the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Article 10 of this constitutional law says that: "Citizens are equal in relation to their rights and duties ..." As it turned out, Mr. Hadzic, can't we agree that Croatian citizens and other non-Serbs who lived in the territory of the SBWS were not equal in terms of their rights, their liberty, particularly the right to stay safe in their own homes. As it turned out, they were not equal, were they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, me, personally, and the government that I represented, they -- people were all equal. However, there were cases where our influence was non-existent and when this was not enforceable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were people who lived there, say, descendants of Croats who had come from Herzegovina after World War II, were those people equal in the SBWS, or were they singled out and made to leave?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were equal. Those who stayed didn't have to leave if they didn't want to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we go to Article 19, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, here we see, again on the 25th of September, 1991, in the constitutional law the provision that sets out the authority, the competencies of the Great National Assembly.
